entries.a229bc8c02f8b7c2978065cc60ed42a2c7c893a0: <div sID="gen20728" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Hag.2" sID="Hag.2"/> <div eID="gen20728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20729" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20730" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have three sermons preached by the prophet Haggai for the encouragement of those that are forward to build the temple. In the first he assures the builders that the glory of the house they were now building should, in spiritual respects, though not in outward, exceed that of Solomon's temple, in which he has an eye to the coming of Christ, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1-Hab.2.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. In the second he assures them that though their sin, in delaying to build the temple, had retarded the prosperous progress of all their other affairs, yet now that they had set about it in good earnest he would bless them, and give them success, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.10-Hab.2.19">ver. 10-19</reference>. In the third he assures Zerubbabel that, as a reward of his pious zeal and activity herein, he should be a favourite of Heaven, and one of the ancestors of Messiah the Prince, whose kingdom should be set up on the ruins of all opposing powers, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.20-Hab.2.23">ver. 20-23</reference>.
entries.be057a2f546b90c443303f8976b428a237dacd00: <div eID="gen20730" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20729" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Latter House. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In the seventh <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the one and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by the prophet Haggai, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, and to the residue of the people, saying, <hi type="super">3</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing? <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and work: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with you, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">According to</hi> the word that I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt, so my spirit remaineth among you: fear ye not. <hi type="super">6</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Yet once, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry <hi type="italic">land;</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will shake all nations, and the desire of all nations shall come: and I will fill this house with glory, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">8</hi> The silver <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, and the gold <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">9</hi> The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen20731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20732" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The date of this message, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.1">v. 1</reference>. It was sent on the twenty-first day of the seventh month, when the builders had been about a month at work (since the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month), and had got it in some forwardness. Note, Those that are hearty in the service of God shall receive fresh encouragements from him to proceed in it, as their case calls for them. Set the wheels a going, and God will oil them. <div eID="gen20732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20733" type="x-p"/> II. The direction of this message, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.2">v. 2</reference>. The encouragements here are sent to the same persons to whom the reproofs in the foregoing chapter are directed; for those that are wounded by the convictions of the word shall be healed and bound up by its consolations. <hi type="italic">Speak to Zerubbabel, and Joshua, and the residue of the people,</hi> the very same that <hi type="italic">obeyed the voice of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.12">ch. i. 12</reference>) and whose spirits God stirred up to do so (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">ch. i. 14</reference>); to them are sent these words of comfort. <div eID="gen20733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20734" type="x-p"/> III. The message itself, in which observe, <div eID="gen20734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20735" type="x-p"/> 1. The discouragements which those laboured under who were employed in this work. That which was such a damp upon them, and an alloy to their joy, when the foundation of the temple was laid, was still a clog upon them—that they could not build such a temple now as Solomon built, not so large, so stately, so sumptuous, a one as that was. This fetched tears from the eyes of many, when the dimensions of it were first laid (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezra iii. 12</reference>), and still it made the work go on heavily—that the glory of this house, <hi type="italic">in comparison</hi> with that of the former, was <hi type="italic">as nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">v. 3</reference>. It was now about seventy years since Solomon's temple was destroyed (for that was in the nineteenth year of the captivity, and this about the nineteenth after the captivity), so that there might be some yet alive who could remember to have seen it, and still they would be upbraiding themselves and their brethren with the great disparity between this house and that. One could remember the gold with which it was overlaid, another the precious stones with which it was garnished; one could describe the magnificence of the porch, another of the pillars—and where are these now? This weakened the hands of the builders; for, though our gracious God is pleased with us if we do in sincerity as well as we can in his service, yet our proud hearts will scarcely let us be pleased with ourselves unless we do as well as others whose abilities far exceed ours. And it is sometimes the fault of old people to discourage the services of the present age by crying up too much the performances and attainments of the former age, with which others should be provoked to emulation, but not exposed to contempt. <hi type="italic">Say not thou that the former days were better than these</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Eccl. vii. 10</reference>), but thank God that there is any good in these, bad as they are. <div eID="gen20735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20736" type="x-p"/> 2. The encouragement that is given them to go on in the work, notwithstanding (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet now,</hi> though this house is likely to be much inferior to the former, <hi type="italic">be strong, O Zerubbabel! and be strong, O Joshua!</hi> Let not these leading men give way to this suggestion, nor be disheartened by it, but do as well as they can, when they cannot do so well as they would; and let <hi type="italic">all the people of the land be strong</hi> too, <hi type="italic">and work;</hi> and, if the leaders have but a good heart on it, it is hoped that the followers will have the better heart. Note, Those that work for God ought to exert themselves with vigour, and then to encourage themselves with hope that it will end well. <div eID="gen20736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20737" type="x-p"/> 3. The grounds of these encouragements. God himself says to them, <hi type="italic">Fear you not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.5">v. 5</reference>), and he gives good reasons for it. <div eID="gen20737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20738" type="x-p"/> (1.) They have God with them, his Spirit and his special presence: <hi type="italic">Be strong, for I am with you, saith the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.2.4">v. 4</reference>. This he had said before (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.13">ch. i. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am with you.</hi> But we need to have these assurances repeated, that we may have strong consolation. The presence of God with us, as the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts,</hi> is enough to silence all our fears and to help us over all the discouragements we may meet with in the way of our duty. The Jews had hosts against them, but they had the Lord of hosts with them, to take their part and plead their cause. He is with them; for, [1.] He adheres to his promise. His covenant is inviolable, and he will be always theirs, and will appear and act for them, <hi type="italic">according to the word that he covenanted with them when they came out of Egypt.</hi> Though <hi type="italic">he chastens them for their transgressions with the rod,</hi> yet he will not make his faithfulness to fail. [2.] He dwells among them by his Spirit, the Spirit of prophecy. When he first formed them into a people <hi type="italic">he gave his good Spirit to instruct them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.20">Neh. ix. 20</reference>); and still the Spirit, though often grieved and provoked to withdraw, remained among them. It was the Spirit of God that stirred up their spirits to come out of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezra i. 5</reference>), and now to build the temple, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">Hag. i. 14</reference>. Note, We have reason to be encouraged as long as we have the Spirit of God remaining among us to work upon us, for so long we have God with us to work for us. <div eID="gen20738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20739" type="x-p"/> (2.) They shall have the Messiah among them shortly—<hi type="italic">him that should come.</hi> To him bore all the prophets witness and this prophet particularly here, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6-Hag.2.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Here is an intimation of the time of his coming, that it should not be long ere he came: "<hi type="italic">Yet once, it is a little while,</hi> and he shall come. The Old-Testament church has but one stage more (if we may say so) to travel; five stages were now past, from Adam to Noah, thence to Abraham, thence to Moses, thence to Solomon's temple, thence to the captivity, and now yet one stage more, its sixth day's journey, and then comes the sabbatism of the Messiah's kingdom. Let the Son of man, when he comes, find faith on the earth, and let the children of promise continue still looking for him, for now it is but <hi type="italic">a little while</hi> and he will come; <hi type="italic">hold out, faith and patience,</hi> yet awhile, for <hi type="italic">he that shall come will come, and will not tarry.</hi>" And, as he then said of his first appearance, so now of his second, <hi type="italic">Surely I come quickly.</hi> Now concerning his coming it is here foretold, [1.] That it shall be introduced by a general shaking (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land.</hi> This is applied to the setting up of Christ's kingdom in the world, to make way for which he will <hi type="italic">judge among the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 6</reference>. God will once again do for his church as he did when he brought them out of Egypt; he shook the heavens and earth at Mount Sinai, with thunder, and lightnings, and earthquakes; he shook the sea and the dry land when lanes were made through the sea and streams fetched out of the rock. This shall be done again, when, at the sufferings of Christ, the sun shall be darkened, the earth shake, the rocks rend—when, at the birth of Christ, Herod and all <hi type="italic">Jerusalem are troubled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.3">Matt. ii. 3</reference>), and he is <hi type="italic">set for the fall and rising again of many.</hi> When his kingdom was set up it was with a shock to the nations; the oracles were silenced, idols were destroyed, and the powers of the kingdoms were moved and removed, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">Heb. xii. 27</reference>. It denotes <hi type="italic">the removing of the things that are shaken.</hi> Note, The shaking of the nations is often in order to the settling of the church and the establishing of the things that cannot be shaken. [2.] That it shall issue in a general satisfaction. He shall come as <hi type="italic">the desire of all nations</hi>—desirable to all nations, for <hi type="italic">in him shall all the families of the earth be blessed</hi> with the best of blessings—long expected and desired by the good people in all nations, that had any intelligence from the Old-Testament predictions concerning him. Balaam in the land of Moab had spoken of a star that should arise out of Jacob, and Job in the land of Uz of his living Redeemer; the concourse of devout men from all parts at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.5">Acts ii. 5</reference>) was in expectation of the setting up of the Messiah's kingdom about that time. All the nations that are brought in to Christ, and discipled in his name, have called him, and will call him, <hi type="italic">all their salvation and all their desire.</hi> This glorious title of Christ seems to refer to Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>), that <hi type="italic">to him shall the gathering of the people be.</hi> <div eID="gen20739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20740" type="x-p"/> (3.) The house they are now building shall be filled with glory to such a degree that its glory shall exceed that of Solomon's temple. The enemies of the Jews followed them with reproach, and cast contempt upon the house they were building; but they might very well endure that when God undertook to fill it with glory. It is God's prerogative to fill with glory; the glory that comes from him is satisfying, and not vain glory. Moses's tabernacle and Solomon's temple were filled with glory when God in a cloud took possession of them; but this house shall be filled with glory of another nature. [1.] Let them not be concerned because this house will not have so much silver and gold about it as Solomon's temple had, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">v. 8</reference>. God needs not the silver and gold to adorn his temple, for (says he), <hi type="italic">The silver is mine, and the gold is mine.</hi> All the silver and gold in the world are his; all that is hid in the bowels of the earth (for <hi type="italic">the earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof</hi>), all that is laid up in the exchequers, banks, and treasuries of the children of men, and all that circulates for the maintaining of trade and commerce; it is all <hi type="italic">the Lord's.</hi> Every penny bears his image as well as Cæsar's; and therefore when gold and silver are dedicated to his honour, and employed in his service, no addition is made to him, for it was his before. When David and his princes offered vast sums for the service of the house of God, they acknowledged, <hi type="italic">It is all thy own, and of thy own, Lord, have we given thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">1 Chron. xxix. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.16">16</reference>. Therefore God needs not sacrifice, for <hi type="italic">every beast of the forest is his,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.10">Ps. l. 10</reference>. Note, If we have silver and gold, we must serve and honour God with them, for they are all his own, we have but the use of them, the property remains in him; but, if we have not silver and gold to honour him with, we must honour him with such as we have, and he will accept us, for he needs them not; all the <hi type="italic">silver and gold</hi> in the world are his already. <hi type="italic">The earth is full of his riches,</hi> so <hi type="italic">is the great and wide sea also.</hi> [2.] Let them be comforted with this, that, though this temple have less gold in it, it shall have more glory than Solomon's (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former.</hi> This was never true in respect of outward glory. This latter house was indeed in its latter times very much beautified and enriched by Herod, and we find the disciples admiring the stones and buildings of the temple, how fine they were (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">Mark xiii. 1</reference>); but it was nothing in comparison with Solomon's temple; and, besides, the Jews own that several of the divine glories of the first temple were wanting in this—the <hi type="italic">ark,</hi> the <hi type="italic">urim</hi> and <hi type="italic">thummim,</hi> the <hi type="italic">fire from heaven,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Schechinah;</hi> so that we cannot conceive how the glory of this latter house should in any thing exceed that of the former, but in that which would indeed excel all the glories of the first house—the presence of the Messiah in it, the Son of God, his being presented there <hi type="italic">the glory of his people Israel,</hi> his attending there at twelve years old, and afterwards his preaching and working miracles there, and his driving the buyers and sellers out of it. It was necessary, then, that the Messiah should come while the second temple stood; but, that being long since destroyed, we must conclude that our Lord Jesus is the Christ, is <hi type="italic">he that should come,</hi> and we are to <hi type="italic">look for no other.</hi> It was also the <hi type="italic">glory of this latter house, First,</hi> That, before the coming of Christ, it was always kept free from idols and idolatries, and was never polluted with those abominable things, as the first temple often was (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11-2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings xxiii. 11, 12</reference>), and in this its glory excelled all the glory of that. Note, The purity of the church, and the strict adherence to divine institutions, are much more its glory than external pomp and splendour. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That, after Christ, the gospel was preached in it by the apostles, even all the words of this life, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.20">Acts v. 20</reference>. In the temple Jesus Christ was daily preached, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.42">Acts v. 42</reference>. Now the ministration of righteousness and life by the gospel was unspeakably more glorious than the law, which was a <hi type="italic">ministration of death and condemnation,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9-2Cor.3.10">2 Cor. iii. 9, 10</reference>. Note, That is the most valuable glory which arises from our relation to Christ and our interest in him. As, where Christ is, <hi type="italic">behold a greater than Solomon is there,</hi> so the heart in which he dwells, and makes a living temple, behold it is more glorious than Solomon's temple, and will be so to eternity. <div eID="gen20740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20741" type="x-p"/> (4.) They should see a comfortable end of their present troubles, and enjoy the pleasure of a happy settlement: <hi type="italic">In this place will I give peace, saith the Lord of hosts.</hi> Note, God's presence with his people in his ordinances secures to them all good. If God be with us, peace is with us. But the Jews under the latter temple had so much trouble that we must conclude this promise to have its accomplishment in that spiritual peace which Jesus Christ has by his blood purchased for, and by his last will and testament bequeathed to, all believers (<reference osisRef="John.14.27">John xiv. 27</reference>), that peace which Christ himself preached as the prophet of peace, and gives as the prince of peace. God will <hi type="italic">give peace in this place;</hi> he will give his Son to be the peace, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>.
entries.7ed30326aa4f6746a4e4191837b6cdc85f95e5f2: <div eID="gen20741" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evil More Communicable than Good; Encouragement to Build the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  520.)</title> <div sID="gen20742" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> In the four and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the ninth <hi type="italic">month,</hi> in the second year of Darius, came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by Haggai the prophet, saying, <hi type="super">11</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Ask now the priests <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> the law, saying, <hi type="super">12</hi> If one bear holy flesh in the skirt of his garment, and with his skirt do touch bread, or pottage, or wine, or oil, or any meat, shall it be holy? And the priests answered and said, No. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then said Haggai, If <hi type="italic">one that is</hi> unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean? And the priests answered and said, It shall be unclean. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then answered Haggai, and said, So <hi type="italic">is</hi> this people, and so <hi type="italic">is</hi> this nation before me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and so <hi type="italic">is</hi> every work of their hands; and that which they offer there <hi type="italic">is</hi> unclean. <hi type="super">15</hi> And now, I pray you, consider from this day and upward, from before a stone was laid upon a stone in the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">16</hi> Since those <hi type="italic">days</hi> were, when <hi type="italic">one</hi> came to a heap of twenty <hi type="italic">measures,</hi> there were <hi type="italic">but</hi> ten: when <hi type="italic">one</hi> came to the press-fat for to draw out fifty <hi type="italic">vessels</hi> out of the press, there were <hi type="italic">but</hi> twenty. <hi type="super">17</hi> I smote you with blasting and with mildew and with hail in all the labours of your hands; yet ye <hi type="italic">turned</hi> not to me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> Consider now from this day and upward, from the four and twentieth day of the ninth <hi type="italic">month, even</hi> from the day that the foundation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's temple was laid, consider <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> Is the seed yet in the barn? yea, as yet the vine, and the fig tree, and the pomegranate, and the olive tree, hath not brought forth: from this day will I bless <hi type="italic">you.</hi> <div eID="gen20742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20743" type="x-p"/> This sermon was preached two months after that in the former part of the chapter. The priests and Levites preached constantly, but the prophets preached occasionally; both were good and needful. We have need to be taught our duty <hi type="italic">in season and out of season.</hi> The people were now going on vigorously with the building of the temple, and in hopes shortly to have it ready for their use and to be employed in the services of it; and now God sends them a message by his prophet, which would be of use to them. <div eID="gen20743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20744" type="x-p"/> I. By way of conviction and caution. They were now engaged in a very good work, but they were concerned to see to it, not only that it was good for the matter of it, but that it was done in a right manner, for otherwise it would not be accepted of God. God sees there are many among them that spoil this good work, by going about it with unsanctified hearts and hands, and are likely to gain no advantage to themselves by it; these are here convicted, and all are warned thereby to purify the hands they employ in this work, for <hi type="italic">to the pure</hi> only <hi type="italic">all things are pure,</hi> and from the pure only that comes which is pure. This matter is here illustrated by the established rules of the ceremonial law, in putting <hi type="italic">a difference between the clean and the unclean,</hi> about which many of the appointments of the law were conversant. Hereby it appears that a spiritual use is to be made of the ceremonial law, and that it was intended, not only as a divine ritual to the Jews, but for <hi type="italic">instruction in righteousness</hi> to all, even to us upon whom the ends of the world have come, to discover to us both sin and Christ, both our disease and our remedy. Now observe here, <div eID="gen20744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20745" type="x-p"/> 1. What the rule of the law was. The prophet is ordered to enquire of the priests concerning it (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.11">v. 11</reference>); for their <hi type="italic">lips</hi> should <hi type="italic">keep</hi> this <hi type="italic">knowledge,</hi> and the people should <hi type="italic">enquire the law at their mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.7">Mal. ii. 7</reference>. Haggai himself, though a prophet, must <hi type="italic">ask the priests concerning the law.</hi> His business, as an extraordinary messenger, was to expound the providences of God, and to give directions concerning particular duties, as he had done, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.8-Hag.1.9">ch. i. 8, 9</reference>. But he would not take the priests' work out of the hands of those who were the ordinary ministers, and whose business it was to expound the ordinances of God, to teach the people the meaning of them, and to give the general rules for the observance of them. In a case of that nature, Haggai must himself consult them. Note, God has given to his ministers diversities of gifts, and calls them out to do diversities of services, so that they have need one of another, should make use one of another, and be helpful one to another. The prophet, though divinely inspired, cannot say to the priest, <hi type="italic">I have no need of thee,</hi> nor can the priest say so to the prophet. Perhaps Haggai was <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> ordered to consult the priests, that out of their own mouths he might judge both them and the people committed to their charge, and convict them of worse than ceremonial pollution. See <reference osisRef="Lev.10.10-Lev.10.11">Lev. x. 10, 11</reference>. Now the rules of the law, in the cases propounded, are, (1.) That he that has holy flesh in his clothes cannot by the touch of his clothes communicate holiness (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">If one bear holy flesh in the skirt of his garment,</hi> though the garment is thereby so far made a devoted thing as that it is not to be put to common use till it has first been washed in the holy place (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.27">Lev. vi. 27</reference>), yet it shall by no means transmit a holiness to either meat or drink, so as to make it ever the better to those that use it. (2.) That he that is ceremonially unclean by the touch of a dead body does by his touch communicate that uncleanness. The law is express (<reference osisRef="Num.19.22">Num. xix. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">Whatsoever the unclean person touches shall be unclean;</hi> yet this Haggai will have from the priests' own mouth, for concerning those things that we find very plain in our Bibles yet it is good to have the advice of our ministers. The sum of these two rules is that pollution is more easily communicated than sanctification; that is (says Grotius), There are many ways of vice, but only one of virtue, and that a difficult one. <hi type="italic">Bonum oritur ex integris; malum ex quolibet defectu—Good implies perfection; evil commences with the slightest defect.</hi> Let not men think that living among good people will recommend them to God if they are not good themselves, but let them fear that touching the unclean thing will defile them, and therefore let them keep at a distance from it. <div eID="gen20745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20746" type="x-p"/> 2. How it is here applied (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">So is this people, and so is this nation, before me.</hi> He does not call them his people and his nation (they are unworthy to be owned by him), but <hi type="italic">this people,</hi> and <hi type="italic">this nation.</hi> They have been thus before God; they thought their offering sacrifices on the altar would sanctify them, and excuse their neglect to build the temple, and remove the curse which by that neglect they had brought upon their common enjoyments: "No," says God, "your holy flesh and your altar will be so far from sanctifying your meat and drink, your wine and oil, to you, that your contempt of God's temple will bring a pollution, not only on your common enjoyments, but even on your sacrifices too; so that while you continued in that neglect all was unclean to you, nay, and <hi type="italic">so is this people</hi> still; and so they will be; on these terms they will still stand with me, and on no other—that if they be profane, and sensual, and morally impure, if they have wicked hearts, and live wicked lives, though they work ever so hard at the temple while it is building, and though they offer ever so many and costly sacrifices there when it is built, yet that shall not serve to sanctify their meat and drink to them, and to give them a comfortable use of them; nay, the impurity of their hearts and lives shall make even that work of their hands, and all their offerings, unclean, and an abomination to God." And the case is the same with us. Those whose devotions are plausible, but whose conversation is wicked, will find their devotions unable to sanctify their enjoyments, but their wickedness prevailing to pollute them. Note, When we are employed in any good work we should be jealous over ourselves, lest we render it unclean by our corruptions and mismanagements. <div eID="gen20746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20747" type="x-p"/> II. By way of comfort and encouragement. If their hearts be right with God, and their eye single in his service, they shall have the benefit of their devotion. God will take away the judgment of famine wherewith they have been corrected for their remissness, and will restore them great plenty. This they are called to consider, and to observe whether God would not be to the utmost as good as his word, and by his providence remarkably countenance and recompense their reformation in this matter. To make this the more signal, let them set down the day when they began to work at the building of the temple, to raise the structure upon the foundations that had been laid some time before. On the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month they began to prepare materials (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.15">ch. i. 15</reference>), and now on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month they began to <hi type="italic">lay a stone upon a stone in the temple of the Lord;</hi> let them take notice of this day, and observe, 1. How they had gone behind-hand in their estates before this day. Let them remember the time when there was a sensible waste and decay in all they had, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.16">v. 16</reference>. A man went to his garner, expecting to find <hi type="italic">a heap of twenty measures</hi> of corn, so much he used to have from such a piece of ground, or so much used to be left at that time of the year, or so much he took it for granted there was when he fetched the last from it, but he found it unaccountably diminished, and, when he came to measure it, <hi type="italic">there were but ten</hi> measures; it had run in and dried away in the keeping, or vermin had eaten it, or it was stolen. In like manner he went to <hi type="italic">the wine-press,</hi> expecting to draw <hi type="italic">fifty vessels</hi> of wine, for so much he used to have from such a quantity of grapes, but they did not yield as usual, for he could get <hi type="italic">but twenty.</hi> This agrees with what we had, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">ch. i. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">You looked for much, and it came to little.</hi> Note, It is our folly that we are apt to raise our expectation from the creature, and to think tomorrow must needs be as this day and much more abundant, but we are commonly disappointed, and the more we expect the more grievous the disappointment is. In the stores and treasures of the new covenant we need not fear being disappointed when we come by faith to draw from them. But this was not all. God did visibly contend with them in the weather (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">I smote you with blastings,</hi> winds and frosts, which made every green thing to wither, <hi type="italic">and with mildew,</hi> which choked the corn when it was knitting, <hi type="italic">and with hail,</hi> which battered it down and broke it when it had grown to some maturity; thus they were disappointed <hi type="italic">in all the labour of their hands,</hi> while they neglected to lay their hand to the work of God and to labour in that. Note, While we take no care of God's interest we cannot expect he should take care of ours. And, when he thus walks contrary to us, he expects that we should return to him and to our duty. But this people either saw not the hand of God in it (imputing it to chance) or saw not their own sin as the provoking cause of it, and therefore turned not to him. They were a long time incorrigible and unhumbled under these rebukes, so that God's hand was <hi type="italic">stretched out still,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the people turned not to him that smote them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12-Isa.9.13">Isa. ix. 12, 13</reference>. They might easily observe that as long as they continued in neglect of the temple work all their affairs went backward. But, 2. Let them now observe, and they should find that from this day forward God would bless them (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.18-Hag.2.19">v. 18, 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Consider now</hi> whether when you begin to change you way towards God you do not find God changing his way towards you; from <hi type="italic">this day,</hi> when you fall to work about the temple, <hi type="italic">consider it,</hi> I say, and you shall find a remarkable turn given for the better to all your affairs. <hi type="italic">Is the seed yet in the barn?</hi> Yes it is, and not yet thrown into the ground. The fruit-trees do not as yet bud, <hi type="italic">the vine, and the fig-tree, and the olive-tree,</hi> have not as <hi type="italic">yet brought forth,</hi> so that nothing appears to promise a good harvest or vintage next year. Nature does not promise it; but now that you begin to apply in good earnest to your duty, the God of nature promises it; he has said, <hi type="italic">From this day I will bless you.</hi> It is the best day's work you ever did in your lives, for hence you may date the return of your prosperity." He does not say what they shall be, but, in general, <hi type="italic">I will bless you;</hi> and those that know what are the fruits flowing from God's blessing know they can desire no more to make them happy. "<hi type="italic">I will bless you,</hi> and then you shall soon recover all your losses, shall thrive as fast as before you went backward; for <hi type="italic">the blessing of the Lord, that maketh rich,</hi> and those <hi type="italic">whom he blesses are blessed indeed.</hi>" Note, When we begin to make conscience of our duty to God we may expect his blessing; and this tree of life is so known by its fruits that one may discern almost to a day a remarkable turn of Providence in favour of those that return in a way of duty; so that they and others may say that <hi type="italic">from this day they are blessed.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Mal.3.10">Mal. iii. 10</reference>. And <hi type="italic">whoso is wise will observe these things, and understand</hi> by them <hi type="italic">the lovingkindness of the Lord.</hi>
entries.a1d884078dc7091d3a1c5d00a1c461c0109c55fc: <div eID="gen20747" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouraging Promises; A Promise to Zerubbabel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen20748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And again the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Haggai in the four and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, saying, <hi type="super">21</hi> Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I will shake the heavens and the earth; <hi type="super">22</hi> And I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms, and I will destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the heathen; and I will overthrow the chariots, and those that ride in them; and the horses and their riders shall come down, every one by the sword of his brother. <hi type="super">23</hi> In that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen20748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20749" type="x-p"/> After Haggai's sermon <hi type="italic">ad populum</hi>—<hi type="italic">to the people,</hi> here follows one, the same day, <hi type="italic">ad magistratum</hi>—<hi type="italic">to the magistrates,</hi> a word directed particularly to <hi type="italic">Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah,</hi> who was a leading active man in this good work which the people now set about, and therefore he shall have some particular marks put upon him (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah,</hi> speak to him by himself. He has thoughts in his head far above those of the common people, as wise princes are wont to have, who move in a higher and larger sphere than others. The people of the land are in care about their corn-fields and vineyards; God has assured them that they shall prosper, and we hope that will make them easy; but Zerubbabel is concerned about the community and its interests, about the neighbouring nations, and the revolutions of their governments, and what will become of the few and feeble Jews in those changes and convulsions, and how such a poor prince as he is should be able to keep his ground and serve his country. "Go to him," says God, "and tell him it shall be well with him and his remnant, and let that make him easy." <div eID="gen20749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20750" type="x-p"/> I. Let him expect to hear of great commotions in the nations of the earth, and let them not be a surprise to him; behold, he is told of them before (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.21-Hag.2.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will shake the heavens and the earth.</hi> This he had said before (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6-Hag.2.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), and now says it again to Zerubbabel; let him expect shaking times, universal concussions. The world is like the sea, like the wheel, always in motion, but sometimes in a special manner turbulent. But, Blessed be God, if the earth be shaken, it is to <hi type="italic">shake the wicked out of it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 13</reference>. In the apocalyptic visions earthquakes bode no ill to the church. Here the heavens and the earth are shaken, that proud oppressors may be broken and brought down: <hi type="italic">I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms.</hi> The Chaldean monarchy, which had been the throne of kingdoms a great while, was already overthrown; and the powers that are, and are yet to come, shall in like manner be overthrown; their day will come to fall. 1. Though they be ever so powerful, yet the <hi type="italic">strength of their kingdoms</hi> shall be destroyed. They <hi type="italic">trust in chariots and horses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>), but their <hi type="italic">chariots</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">overthrown,</hi> and <hi type="italic">those that ride in them,</hi> so that they shall not be able to attack the people of God, whom they persecute, not to escape the judgments of God, which persecute them. 2. Though there appear none likely to be the instruments of their destruction, yet God will bring it about, for they shall be brought down <hi type="italic">every one by the sword of his brother.</hi> This reads the doom of all the enemies of God's church, that will not repent to give him glory; it seems likewise designed as a promise of Christ's victory over the powers of darkness, his overthrow of Satan's throne, that <hi type="italic">throne of kingdoms,</hi> the throne of the god of this world, the taking from him all the armour wherein he trusted and <hi type="italic">dividing the spoil.</hi> And all opposing <hi type="italic">rule, principality, and power,</hi> shall be put down, that the <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> may be <hi type="italic">delivered up to God, even the Father.</hi> <div eID="gen20750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20751" type="x-p"/> II. Let him depend upon it that he shall be safe under the divine protection in the midst of all these commotions, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">v. 23</reference>. Zerubbabel was active to build God a house, and therefore God makes the same promise to him as he did to David on the like occasion—that he would <hi type="italic">build him a house,</hi> and establish it, even <hi type="italic">in that day</hi> when heaven and earth are shaken. This promise refers to this good man himself and to his family. He honoured God, and God would honour him. His successors likewise in the government of Judah might take encouragement from it; though their authority was very precarious as to men, yet God would confirm it, and this would contribute to the stability of the people over whom God had set them. But this promise has special reference to Christ, who lineally descended from Zerubbabel, and is the sole builder of the gospel-temple. 1. Zerubbabel is here owned as <hi type="italic">God's servant,</hi> and it is an honourable mention that is hereby made of him, as Moses and David <hi type="italic">my servants.</hi> When God destroys his enemies he will prefer his servants. Our Lord Jesus is his Father's servant in the work of redemption, but faithful as a Son, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>. 2. He is owned as God's elect: <hi type="italic">I have chosen thee</hi> to this office; and whom God makes choice of he will make use of. Our Lord Jesus is chosen of God, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4">1 Pet. ii. 4</reference>. And he is the head of the chosen remnant; in him they are chosen. 3. It is promised that, being chosen, God will make him <hi type="italic">as a signet.</hi> Jeconiah had been as the <hi type="italic">signet on God's right hand,</hi> but was <hi type="italic">plucked thence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jer. xxii. 24</reference>); and now Zerubbabel is substituted in the room of him. He shall be near and dear to God, precious in his sight, and honourable, and his family shall continue till the Messiah spring out of it, who is <hi type="italic">the signet on God's right hand.</hi> This intimates, (1.) The delight the Father has in him. In him he once and again declared himself to be <hi type="italic">well pleased.</hi> He is set as a <hi type="italic">seal upon his heart, a seal upon his arm,</hi> is brought near unto him (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>), is <hi type="italic">hidden in the shadow of his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.2">Isa. xlix. 2</reference>. (2.) The dominion the Father has entrusted him with. Princes sign their edicts, grants, and commissions, with their signet-rings, <reference osisRef="Esth.3.10">Esth. iii. 10</reference>. Our Lord Jesus is the signet on God's right hand, for all power is given to him and derived from him. By him the great charter of the gospel is signed and ratified, and it is in him that all the promises of God are yea and amen.  <chapter eID="Hag.2"/> <div eID="gen20751" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen20711" osisID="Hag" type="book"/>

entries.e0293670c080528939f2e982c351c88183fc0581: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12988"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hag.2.1-Hag.2.9">Hag 2:1-9</reference>. Second Prophecy. The people, discouraged at the inferiority of this temple to Solomon's, are encouraged nevertheless to persevere, because God is with them, and this house by its connection with Messiah's kingdom shall have a glory far above that of gold and silver.</title> <div sID="gen24367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12988"/><hi type="bold">1. seventh month--</hi>of the Hebrew year; in the second year of Darius' reign (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag 1:1</reference>); not quite a month after they had begun the work (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.15">Hag 1:15</reference>). This prophecy was very shortly before that of Zechariah. <div eID="gen24367" type="x-p"/>
entries.b19417c4c9442baf13cb218e035a692512ae2a1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12989"/><div sID="gen24368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12989"/><hi type="bold">3. Who is left ... that saw ... first glory--</hi>Many elders present at the laying of the foundation of the second temple who had seen the first temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>) in all its glory, wept at the contrast presented by the rough and unpromising appearance of the former in its beginnings. From the destruction of the first temple to the second year of Darius Hystaspes, the date of Haggai's prophecy, was a space of seventy years (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>); and to the first year of Cyrus, or the end of the captivity, fifty-two years; so that the elders might easily remember the first temple. The Jews note five points of inferiority: The absence from the second temple of (1) the sacred fire; (2) the Shekinah; (3) the ark and cherubim; (4) the Urim and Thummim; (5) the spirit of prophecy. The connection of it with Messiah more than counterbalanced all these; for He is the antitype to all the five (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how do ye see it now?--</hi>God's estimate of things is very different from man's (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.6">Zec 8:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">1Sa 16:7</reference>). However low their estimate of the present temple ("it") from its outward inferiority, God holds it superior (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zec 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>). <div eID="gen24369" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1aec8708e0fd9b6d98d807a6414e8b7f71a05a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12990"/><div sID="gen24370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12990"/><hi type="bold">4. be strong ... for I am with you--</hi>The greatest strength is to have Jehovah with us as our strength. Not in man's "might," but in that of God's Spirit (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference>). <div eID="gen24370" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bb3ef394667873817b8f2e49bab9f1c7d3c618b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12991"/><div sID="gen24371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12991"/><hi type="bold">5. According to the word that--</hi>literally, "(I am with you) the word (or thing) which I covenanted"; that is, I am with you as I covenanted with you when ye came out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.10">34:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.11">11</reference>). The covenant promise of God to the elect people at Sinai is an additional motive for their persevering. The Hebrew for to "covenant" is literally "to cut," alluding to the sacrificial victims cut in ratification of a covenant.<div eID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so--</hi>or, "and."<div eID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my Spirit remaineth among you--</hi>to strengthen you for the work (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.14">Hag 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference>). The inspiration of Haggai and Zechariah at this time was a specimen of the presence of God's Spirit remaining still with His people, as He had been with Moses and Israel of old (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">Ezr 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Is 63:11</reference>). <div eID="gen24373" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b70952d8eaa3a0e1a9e90498b59a374747e11cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12992"/><div sID="gen24374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12992"/><hi type="bold">6. Yet once, it is a little while--</hi>or, "(it is) yet a little while." The Hebrew for "once" expresses the indefinite article "a" [Maurer]. Or, "it is yet only a little while"; literally, "one little," that is, a single brief space till a series of movements is to begin; namely, the shakings of nations soon to begin which are to end in the advent of Messiah, "the desire of all nations" [Moore]. The shaking of nations implies judgments of wrath on the foes of God's people, to precede the reign of the Prince of peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.13">Is 13:13</reference>). The kingdoms of the world are but the scaffolding for God's spiritual temple, to be thrown down when their purpose is accomplished. The transitoriness of all that is earthly should lead men to seek "peace" in Messiah's everlasting kingdom (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">He 12:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">28</reference>) [Moore]. The Jews in Haggai's times hesitated about going forward with the work, through dread of the world power, Medo-Persia, influenced by the craft of Samaria. The prophet assures them this and all other world powers are to fall before Messiah, who is to be associated with this temple; therefore they need fear naught. So <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">He 12:26</reference>, which quotes this passage; the apostle compares the heavier punishment which awaits the disobedient under the New Testament with that which met such under the Old Testament. At the establishment of the Sinaitic covenant, only the earth was shaken to introduce it, but now heaven and earth and all things are to be shaken, that is, along with prodigies in the world of nature, all kingdoms that stand in the way of Messiah's kingdom, "which cannot be shaken," are to be upturned (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Da 2:35</reference>, 44; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>). <reference osisRef="Heb.12.27">He 12:27</reference>, "Yet once more," favors English Version. Paul condenses together the two verses of Haggai (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Hag.2.21">Hag 2:21</reference>, 22), implying that it was one and the same shaking, of which the former verses of Haggai denote the beginning, the latter the end. The shaking began introductory to the first advent; it will be finished at the second. Concerning the former, compare <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.51">27:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.2">28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.2">Ac 2:2</reference>; 4:31; concerning the latter, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.20">Re 16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">20:11</reference> [Bengel]. There is scarcely a prophecy of Messiah in the Old Testament which does not, to some extent at least, refer to His second coming [Sir Isaac Newton]. <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference> mentions the heavens dropping near the mountain (Sinai); but Haggai speaks of the whole created heavens: "Wait only a little while, though the promised event is not apparent yet; for soon will God change things for the better: do not stop short with these preludes and fix your eyes on the present state of the temple [Calvin]. God shook the heavens by the lightnings at Sinai; the earth, that it should give forth waters; the sea, that it should be divided asunder. In Christ's time God shook the heaven, when He spake from it; the earth, when it quaked; the sea, when He commanded the winds and waves [Grotius]. Cicero records at the time of Christ the silencing of the heathen oracles; and Dio, the fall of the idols in the Roman capitol. <div eID="gen24374" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bf6df412f1541084cd70ad6569fb284f2389732: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12993"/><div sID="gen24375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12993"/><hi type="bold">7. shake--</hi>not convert; but cause that agitation which is to precede Messiah's coming as the healer of the nations' agitations. The previous shaking shall cause the yearning "desire" for the Prince of peace. Moore and others translate "the beauty," or "the desirable things (the precious gifts) of all nations shall come" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.6">61:6</reference>). He brings these objections to applying "the desire of all nations" to Messiah: (1) The Hebrew means the quality, not the thing desired, namely, its desirableness or beauty, But the abstract is often put for the concrete. So "a man of desires," that is, one desired or desirable (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.23">Da 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.11">10:11</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">Da 10:3</reference>, Margin). (2) Messiah was not desired by all nations, but "a root out of a dry ground," having "no beauty that we should desire Him" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>). But what is implied is not that the nations definitely desired Him, but that He was the only one to satisfy the yearning desires which all felt unconsciously for a Saviour, shown in their painful rites and bloody sacrifices. Moreover, while the Jews as a nation desired Him not (to which people <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference> refers), the Gentiles, who are plainly pointed out by "all nations," accepted Him; and so to them He was peculiarly desirable. (3) The verb, "shall come," is plural, which requires the noun to be understood in the plural, whereas if Messiah be intended, the noun is singular. But when two nouns stand together, of which one is governed by the other, the verb agrees sometimes in number with the latter, though it really has the former as its nominative, that is, the Hebrew "come" is made in number to agree with "nations," though really agreeing with "the desire." Besides, Messiah may be described as realizing in Himself at His coming "the desires (the noun expressing collectively the plural) of all nations"; whence the verb is plural. So in <reference osisRef="Song.5.16">So 5:16</reference>, "He is altogether lovely," in the Hebrew the same word as here, "all desires," that is, altogether desirable, or the object of desires. (4) <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference>, "The silver is mine," &c.; accords with the translation, "the choice things of all nations" shall be brought in. But <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference> harmonizes quite as well with English Version of <reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>, as the note on eighth verse will show; see on <reference osisRef="Hag.2.8">Hag 2:8</reference>. (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>) the Septuagint and Syriac versions agree with Moore's translation. But Vulgate confirms English Version. So also early Jewish Rabbis before Jerome's time. Plato [Alcibiades, 2] shows the yearning of the Gentiles after a spiritual deliverer: "It is therefore necessary," says Alcibiades on the subject of acceptable worship, "to wait until One teach us how we ought to behave towards the gods and men." Alcibiades replies, "When shall that time arrive, and who shall that Teacher be? For most glad would I be to see such a man." The "good tidings of great joy" were "to all people" (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.10">Lu 2:10</reference>). The Jews, and those in the adjoining nations instructed by them, looked for Shiloh to come unto whom the gathering of the people was to be, from Jacob's prophecy (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>). The early patriarchs, Job (Job 19:25-27; 33:23-26) and Abraham (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>), desired Him.<div eID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill this house with glory--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>). As the first temple was filled with the cloud of glory, the symbol of God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.11">1Ki 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.14">2Ch 5:14</reference>), so this second temple was filled with the "glory" of God (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>) veiled in the flesh (as it were in the cloud) at Christ's first coming, when He entered it and performed miracles there (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.12-Matt.21.14">Mt 21:12-14</reference>); but that "glory" is to be revealed at His second coming, as this prophecy in its ulterior reference foretells (Mal 3:1). The Jews before the destruction of Jerusalem all expected Messiah would appear in the second temple. Since that time they invent various forced and false interpretations of such plain Messianic prophecies. <div eID="gen24376" type="x-p"/>
entries.91a4eb0409b01f4e5cd7041a402db1b9b8cad595: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12994"/><div sID="gen24377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12994"/><hi type="bold">8. The silver is mine--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.41.11">Job 41:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.12">Psa 50:12</reference>). Ye are disappointed at the absence of these precious metals in the adorning of this temple, as compared with the first temple: If I pleased I could adorn this temple with them, but I will adorn it with a "glory" (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>) far more precious; namely, with the presence of My divine Son in His veiled glory first, and at His second coming with His revealed glory, accompanied with outward adornment of gold and silver, of which the golden covering within and without put on by Herod is the type. Then shall the nations bring offerings of those precious metals which ye now miss so much (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>; 60:3, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.7">6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">Eze 43:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.5">4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4">44:4</reference>). The heavenly Jerusalem shall be similarly adorned, but shall need "no temple" (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.10-Rev.21.22">Re 21:10-22</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">1Co 3:12</reference>, where gold and silver represent the most precious things (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>). The inward glory of New Testament redemption far exceeds the outward glory of the Old Testament dispensation. So, in the case of the individual poor believer, God, if He pleased, could bestow gold and silver, but He bestows far better treasures, the possession of which might be endangered by that of the former (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jas 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen24377" type="x-p"/>
entries.f370ab738a1deb6b35f04c489efa55a988028f36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12995"/><div sID="gen24378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12995"/><hi type="bold">9. The glory of this latter house ... greater than of the former--</hi>namely, through the presence of Messiah, in (whose) face is given the light of the knowledge of the glory of God (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>), and who said of Himself, "in this place is one greater than the temple" (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.6">Mt 12:6</reference>), and who "sat daily teaching in it" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.55">Mt 26:55</reference>). Though Zerubbabel's temple was taken down to the foundations when Herod rebuilt the temple, the latter was considered, in a religious point of view, as not a third temple, but virtually the second temple.<div eID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in this place ... peace--</hi>namely, at Jerusalem, the metropolis of the kingdom of God, whose seat was the temple: where Messiah "made peace through the blood of His cross" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). Thus the "glory" consists in this "peace." This peace begins by the removal of the difficulty in the way of the just God accepting the guilty (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Psa 85:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">53:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">19</reference>); then it creates peace in the sinner's own heart (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.36">Ac 10:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13-Eph.2.17">Ep 2:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Php 4:7</reference>); then peace in the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>). First peace between God and man, then between man and God, then between man and man (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>). As "Shiloh" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>) means peace, this verse confirms the view that <reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag 2:7</reference>, "the desire of all nations," refers to Shiloh or Messiah, foretold in <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>. <div eID="gen24379" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3c8e09f35c5d1f01a218a7c85770a6c3b96b5ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12996"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hag.2.10-Hag.2.19">Hag 2:10-19</reference>. Third Prophecy. Sacrifices without obedience (in respect to God's command to build the temple) could not sanctify. Now that they are obedient, God will bless them, though no sign is seen of fertility as yet.</title> <div sID="gen24380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12996"/><hi type="bold">10. four and twentieth day ... ninth month--</hi>three days more than two months from the second prophecy (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.1">Hag 2:1</reference>); in the month Chisleu, the lunar one about the time of our December. The Jews seem to have made considerable progress in the work in the interval (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.15-Hag.2.18">Hag 2:15-18</reference>). <div eID="gen24380" type="x-p"/>
entries.aab80be06170958e104ab5aad8476a017d31bf1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12997"/><div sID="gen24381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12997"/><hi type="bold">11. Ask ... the priests--</hi>Propose this question to them on the law. The priests were the authorized expounders of the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.11">Le 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.10">De 33:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.23">Eze 44:23</reference>; Mal 2:7). <div eID="gen24381" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7f3a91a58b1ee8114bc7860d4d9c3ee86ca0e13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12998"/><div sID="gen24382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12998"/>12. "Holy flesh" (that is, the flesh of a sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jr 11:15</reference>), indeed, makes holy the "skirt" in which it is carried; but that "skirt" cannot impart its sanctity to any thing beyond, as "bread," &c. (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.27">Le 6:27</reference>). This is cited to illustrate the principle, that a sacrifice, holy, as enveloping divine things (just as the "skirt" is "holy" which envelops "holy" flesh), cannot by its inherent or opus operatum efficacy make holy a person whose disobedience, as that of the Jew while neglecting God's house, made him unholy. <div eID="gen24382" type="x-p"/>
entries.977d16085300b3e5f34c4d4e6a594e525096bbe5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12999"/><div sID="gen24383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12999"/>13. On the other hand, a legally "unclean" person imparts his uncleanness to any thing, whereas a legally holy thing cannot confer its sanctity on an "unclean" person (<reference osisRef="Num.19.11">Nu 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.22">13, 22</reference>). Legal sanctity is not so readily communicated as legal impurity. So the paths to sin are manifold: the paths to holiness one, and that one of difficult access [Grotius]. One drop of filth will defile a vase of water: many drops of water will not purity a vase of filth [Moore]. <div eID="gen24383" type="x-p"/>
entries.a729325105d703bb86d3635770bf567e9ca5ece7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13000"/><div sID="gen24384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13000"/><hi type="bold">14. Then answered Haggai--</hi>rather, "Then Haggai answered (in rejoinder to the priests' answer) and said" [Maurer].<div eID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so is this people--</hi>heretofore not in such an obedient state of mind as to deserve to be called My people (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>). Here he applies the two cases just stated. By the first case, "this people" is not made "holy" by their offerings "there" (namely, on the altar built in the open air, under Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">Ezr 3:3</reference>); though the ritual sacrifice can ordinarily sanctify outwardly so far as it reaches (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>), as the "holy flesh" sanctified the "skirt," yet it cannot make the offerers in their persons and all their works acceptable to God, because lacking the spirit of obedience (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>) so long as they neglected to build the Lord's house. On the contrary, by the second case, they made "unclean" their very offerings by being unclean through "dead works" (disobedience), just as the person unclean by contact with a dead body imparted his uncleanness to all that he touched (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">He 9:14</reference>). This all applies to them as they had been, not as they are now that they have begun to obey; the design is to guard them against falling back again. The "there" points to the altar, probably in view of the audience which the prophet addressed. <div eID="gen24385" type="x-p"/>
entries.eca3ca879905f77c67c8d4c1bdc8ea307c013c6a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13001"/><div sID="gen24386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13001"/><hi type="bold">15. consider--</hi>literally, "lay it to heart." Ponder earnestly, retracing the past "upward" (that is, backward), comparing what evils heretofore befell you before ye set about this work, with the present time when you have again commenced it, and when in consequence I now engage to "bless you." Hence ye may perceive the evils of disobedience and the blessing of obedience. <div eID="gen24386" type="x-p"/>
entries.076861f9d7772bce45729019ead480472a373647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13002"/><div sID="gen24387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13002"/><hi type="bold">16. Since those days were--</hi>from the time that those days of your neglect of the temple work have been.<div eID="gen24387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when one came to an heap of twenty measures--</hi>that is, to a heap which he had expected would be one of twenty measures, there were but ten.<div eID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fifty vessels out of the press--</hi>As the Septuagint translates "measure," and Vulgate "a flagon," and as we should rather expect vat than press. Maurer translates (omitting vessels, which is not in the original), "purahs," or "wine-measures." <div eID="gen24389" type="x-p"/>
entries.3dc2de90c817b0c26f9d95a5d871f69a8852267f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13003"/><div sID="gen24390" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13003"/>17. Appropriated from <reference osisRef="Amos.4.9">Am 4:9</reference>, whose canonicity is thus sealed by Haggai's inspired authority; in the last clause, "turned," however, has to be supplied, its omission marking by the elliptical abruptness ("yet ye not to Me!") God's displeasure. Compare "(let him come) unto Me!" Moses in excitement omitting the bracketed words (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.26">Ex 32:26</reference>). "Blasting" results from excessive drought; "mildew, from excessive moisture. <div eID="gen24390" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf4be159a496b837e3f904bd159eeaae4de0698c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13004"/><div sID="gen24391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13004"/>18. Resumed from <reference osisRef="Hag.2.15">Hag 2:15</reference> after <reference osisRef="Hag.2.16">Hag 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>, that the blessing in <reference osisRef="Hag.2.19">Hag 2:19</reference> may stand in the more marked contrast with the curse in <reference osisRef="Hag.2.16">Hag 2:16</reference>,<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">17</reference>. Affliction will harden the heart, if not referred to God as its author [Moore].<div eID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even from the day that the foundation of ... temple was laid--</hi>The first foundation beneath the earth had been long ago laid in the second year of Cyrus, 535 B.C. (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10">Ezr 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">11</reference>); the foundation now laid was the secondary one, which, above the earth, was laid on the previous work [Tirinus]. Or, translate, "From this day on which the temple is being begun," namely, on the foundations long ago laid [Grotius]. Maurer translates, "Consider ... from the four and twentieth day ... to (the time which has elapsed) from the day on which the foundation ... was laid." The Hebrew supports English Version. <div eID="gen24392" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0bdc33c752a81b9cee73adc782c3fd5dc5e31f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13005"/><div sID="gen24393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13005"/><hi type="bold">19. Is the seed yet in the barn?--</hi>implying, It is not. It has been already sown this month, and there are no more signs of its bearing a good crop, much less of its being safely stored in the barn, than there were in the past season, when there was such a failure; yet I promise to you from this day (emphatically marking by the repetition the connection of the blessing with the day of their obedience) a blessing in an abundant harvest. So also the vine, &c., which heretofore have borne little or nothing, shall be blessed with productiveness. Thus it will be made evident that the blessing is due to Me, not to nature. We may trust God's promise to bless us, though we see no visible sign of its fulfilment (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Ha 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen24393" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2464156e55f227bd49acadaf75e6b1ceb2e4215: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13006"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hag.2.20-Hag.2.23">Hag 2:20-23</reference>. Fourth Prophecy. God's promise through Zerubbabel to Israel of safety in the coming commotions.</title> <div sID="gen24394" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13006"/><hi type="bold">20. the month--</hi>the ninth in the second year of Darius. The same date as Prophecy III (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.10">Hag 2:10</reference>). <div eID="gen24394" type="x-p"/>
entries.37734c31f42c9281d036d372848163b539d8868c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13007"/><div sID="gen24395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13007"/><hi type="bold">21. to Zerubbabel--</hi>Perhaps Zerubbabel had asked as to the convulsions foretold (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). This is the reply: The Jews had been led to fear that these convulsions would destroy their national existence. Zerubbabel, therefore, as their civil leader and representative is addressed, not Joshua, their religious leader. Messiah is the antitypical Zerubbabel, their national Representative and King, with whom God the Father makes the covenant wherein they, as identified with Him, are assured of safety in God's electing love (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.23">Hag 2:23</reference>, "will make thee as a signet"; "I have chosen thee").<div eID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... heavens--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>); violent political convulsions accompanied with physical prodigies (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mt 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.29">29</reference>). <div eID="gen24396" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f122e0ffc5a5374efe9854431434bb6ae797f0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13008"/><div sID="gen24397" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13008"/>22. All other world kingdoms are to be overthrown to make way for Christ's universal kingdom (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>). War chariots are to give place to His reign of peace (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.10">Mi 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen24397" type="x-p"/>
entries.d65232c27d94375c3b0bf547e68044e9a2c08ae4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13009"/><div sID="gen24398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13009"/><hi type="bold">23. take thee--</hi>under My protection and to promote thee and thy people to honor (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>).<div eID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24399" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a signet--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.8.6">So 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>). A ring with a seal on it; the legal representative of the owner; generally of precious stones and gold, &c., and much valued. Being worn on the finger, it was an object of constant regard. In all which points of view the theocratic people, and their representative, Zerubbabel the type, and Messiah his descendant the Antitype, are regarded by God. The safety of Israel to the end is guaranteed in Messiah, in whom God hath chosen them as His own (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">43:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">44:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">49:3</reference>). So the spiritual Israel is sealed in their covenant head by His Spirit (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>, 13, 14). All is ascribed, not to the merits of Zerubbabel, but to God's gratuitous choice. Christ is the "signet" on God's hand: always in the Father's presence, ever pleasing in his sight. The signet of an Eastern monarch was the sign of delegated authority; so Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.23">23</reference>). <chapter eID="Hag.2"/><div eID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen24320" osisID="Hag" type="book"/>

entries.16da5e1c88f753d8659b4e06306de34f4b111b99: <div eID="gen35363" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35364" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35365" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35365" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35364" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35366" type="x-p"/> When this prophecy was uttered, about four years before the temple was finished, and sixty-eight after the former one was destroyed, it appears that some old men among the Jews were greatly dispirited on account of its being so much inferior in magnificence to that of Solomon. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>. To raise the spirits of the people, and encourage them to proceed with the work, the prophet assures them that the glory of the second temple should be greater than that of the first, alluding perhaps to the glorious doctrines which should be preached in it by Jesus Christ and his apostles, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.1-Hag.2.9">Hag 2:1-9</reference>. He then shows the people that the oblations brought by their priests could not sanctify them while they were unclean by their neglect of the temple; and to convince them that the difficult times they had experienced during that neglect proceeded from this cause, he promises fruitful seasons from that day forward, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.10-Hag.2.19">Hag 2:10-19</reference>. The concluding verses contain a prediction of the mighty revolutions that should take place by the setting up of the kingdom of Christ under the type of Zerubbabel, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.20-Hag.2.23">Hag 2:20-23</reference>. As the time which elapsed between the date of the prophecy and the dreadful concussion of nations is termed in <reference osisRef="Hag.2.6">Hag 2:6</reference>, A Little While, the words may likewise have reference to some temporal revolutions then near, such as the commotions of Babylon in the reign of Darius, the Macedonian conquests in Persia, and the wars between the successors of Alexander; but the aspect of the prophecy is more directly to the amazing victories of the Romans, who, in the time of Haggai and Zechariah, were on the Very Eve of their successful career, and in the lapse of a few centuries subjugated the whole habitable globe; and therefore, in a very good sense, God may be said by these people to have shaken "the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land;" and thus to have prepared the way for the opening of the Gospel dispensation. See <reference osisRef="Heb.12.25-Heb.12.29">Heb 12:25-29</reference>. Others have referred this prophecy to the period of our Lord's second advent, to which there is no doubt it is also applicable; and when it will be in the most signal manner fulfilled.
